title: Animated Ads: Formats, Examples and How to Make Them
summary: Animated ads use motion graphics, GIFs or cartoon characters instead of live footage. Formats, famous examples, specs and how to build one that performs.
body_markdown:
## The short answer


- An **animated ad** uses motion graphics, illustration, 2D or 3D animation, or an animated GIF in place of live-action footage to deliver a marketing message.
- The main formats are animated display banners, animated GIFs, motion graphics, character or cartoon spots, and animated explainers.
- Google Ads accepts animated GIF display ads up to 150 KB, 30 seconds long and slower than 5 frames per second.
- Animation is strongest for abstract products, software and anything that is hard or expensive to film. It is weaker where a real person's face is the proof.


## What animated ads are


An animated ad is any ad where the movement is drawn or generated rather than filmed. That covers a three-frame GIF banner, a 15 second motion graphics clip with a voiceover, a character-led TV spot and a 90 second explainer.


Brands pick animation for three reasons. It can show things a camera cannot, such as how software works or what happens inside a pipe. It keeps a consistent look across dozens of variations. And it can be cheaper to edit: changing a line of text or a colour in an animation file does not require a reshoot.


It sits next to the formats in[types of advertising](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/types-of-advertising) and uses the same persuasion methods as[advertising techniques](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/advertising-techniques) . The difference is the production route, not the strategy.


## Animated ad formats


Five formats cover most of what runs.


Format What it is Where it runs Good for


Animated GIF banner A looping image of a few frames in a standard display size Display networks, email Simple offers, retargeting


Motion graphics ad Animated text, shapes and product images with music or voiceover Social feeds, YouTube, connected TV Feature explainers, launches


Character or cartoon spot A drawn or 3D character carries the story TV, YouTube, social Brand building, family audiences


Animated explainer A 60 to 120 second story of how a product solves a problem Landing pages, video ads Software, finance, B2B


HTML5 animated ad Code-driven animation inside a display ad Display networks Rich banners with interaction


Technical limits differ by platform. For Google Display, the Google Ads Help page "Uploaded display ads specifications" (checked November 9, 2026) says animated and non-animated image ads can be GIF, JPG or PNG up to 150 KB. Animation length must be 30 seconds or shorter, looping is allowed but must stop after 30 seconds, and animated GIFs must be slower than 5 frames per second. The same page says HTML5 ads need an account open for more than 90 days with more than $9,000 USD in lifetime spend. The sizes you can use are in[banner ad sizes](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/banner-ad-sizes) .


## Animated ad examples


These are well-known animated campaigns. The point is what each one does, not how it scored.


- **Chipotle, "Back to the Start" (2011).** A stop-motion animated film about a farmer who leaves industrial farming, set to a Willie Nelson cover. It sold a food-sourcing idea without showing a burrito.
- **Coca-Cola polar bears.** Animated bears have been Coca-Cola holiday characters for decades. A recognisable character carries the brand across years and countries.
- **GEICO gecko.** A 3D animated mascot who delivers a short insurance pitch in a few seconds.
- **Kellogg's Tony the Tiger.** A drawn mascot used in cereal advertising for decades, so the character does the brand recall work.
- **Dropbox animated explainers.** Simple drawn explainers showing how file syncing works, a standard approach for software that is hard to film.
- **Headspace.** Soft, simple animation used to explain meditation, a topic with nothing to point a camera at.


Across these examples the pattern is the same. A single character or visual device, a simple story, and an idea that would be awkward to film. For a library of what is running today, see[ad examples](https://www.sprites.ai/ad-examples) .


## When animation beats live action


Choose animation when:


- The product is abstract: software, data, finance, insurance, health ideas.
- You need many versions fast. Swap text, colour or language in the source file.
- Your audience is broad or global, and a drawn character travels better than a face.
- Filming is expensive, dangerous or impossible.


Choose live action when a real customer's face or a real product in a real hand is the proof. Testimonials, unboxings and demos of physical goods tend to need a person. A common split is animation for the explanation and a real person for the proof.


## How to make an animated ad


1. **Write a one-line promise.** What does the viewer get? Animation does not fix a vague message.
2. **Script it in under 100 words.** A 30 second ad is about 70 to 80 spoken words.
3. **Storyboard six to eight frames.** One idea per frame. Put the hook in frame one.
4. **Choose a style and keep it.** Flat 2D, stop motion, kinetic type or 3D. One style per ad.
5. **Build the motion.** Use a motion tool or an animation freelancer. For GIFs, keep file size and the Google 150 KB cap in mind.
6. **Add sound and captions.** Many people watch muted, so the message must work on screen alone.
7. **Export to each placement.** Different ratios for feed, Stories and display.
8. **Test hooks.** Keep the body, vary the first three seconds, and track[hook rate](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/hook-rate) .


Safe zones and sizes for social placements are on the[Meta specs](https://www.sprites.ai/ad-specs/meta) and[TikTok specs](https://www.sprites.ai/ad-specs/tiktok) pages.


## Mistakes to avoid


- **Too much movement.** A banner where everything animates at once reads as noise. Move one element at a time.
- **A loop that never ends.** Google limits animations to 30 seconds, and a looping banner with no clear final frame has no call to action at rest.
- **Slow openings.** An animated logo reveal spends the hook on nothing. Start with the idea.
- **Generic stock style.** If the animation could be any brand's, it will be forgotten. A distinct character or colour palette is worth the effort.

## Frequently asked questions


### What are animated ads?


Animated ads are ads where the movement is drawn or generated instead of filmed. They include animated GIF banners, motion graphics, cartoon or character spots and animated explainer videos.


### What are some examples of animated ads?


Chipotle's "Back to the Start" stop-motion film, Coca-Cola's polar bears, the GEICO gecko, Kellogg's Tony the Tiger, Dropbox's drawn explainers and Headspace's simple meditation animations.


### What size can an animated GIF ad be on Google Ads?


Google's Help page says animated and non-animated image ads can be GIF, JPG or PNG up to 150 KB. Animations must be 30 seconds or shorter and slower than 5 frames per second.


### Are animated ads more effective than static ads?


There is no universal answer. Animation tends to suit abstract products and gets attention in feeds, but results depend on the hook, the offer and the audience. Test an animated and a static version of the same message.


### How long should an animated ad be?


For social and display, aim for 6 to 30 seconds with the main point in the first three seconds. Explainers on a landing page can run 60 to 120 seconds because viewers have chosen to watch.


### Can I make animated ads without an animator?


Yes. Motion graphics tools, templates and AI video tools can produce simple animated ads. Write the script and storyboard yourself, then generate or assemble the motion and export for each placement.
